title: The Appalachian Trail: A Heckuva Hike
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Appalachian Trail: what a through hike is, its length (about 2,194 miles from Springer Mountain, Georgia to Mount Katahdin, Maine), its history from Benton MacKaye's original idea through Myron Avery's leadership and completion in 1937, and Earl Schaefer's 1948 first through hike. They cover the basics of planning a NOBO or SOBO hike, flip-flopping and leapfrogging, the bubble, blazes, shelters, resupply by mail, food and hiker hunger, gear costs, weather and hypothermia, heat and water, ticks and bears, safety statistics, trail names and trail magic, and records set by Emma "Grandma" Gatewood, Joe McConaughey, Sunny Everhart, Harvey Sutton, Juniper Netteberg and Bill Irwin. The episode ends with a listener email from Kirby about kidney donation.

segments.title: Opening banter and trail names
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about trail names and introduce the Appalachian Trail as a long-requested topic, noting the thru-hike definition and the roughly 2,194-mile length.

segments.title: Length, elevation and thru-hike basics
segments.summary: The hosts explain that about three million people use the trail each year, only a few thousand attempt a thru-hike, and roughly one in four succeed. They compare total elevation change to Mount Everest and note the trail allows no pack animals.

segments.title: Benton MacKaye's original idea
segments.summary: Benton MacKaye, a forester and land use planner, conceived a linked trail from Georgia to Maine after a hike in Vermont's Green Mountains. His 1921 paper also proposed shelters, community camps and labor-union farms.

segments.title: Myron Avery and the trail's completion
segments.summary: Myron Avery, a Washington lawyer and hiker, took charge of the project in 1930 and was known as stubborn and demanding. MacKaye fell out with him and left the project. Avery mapped the trail and it opened to the public after seven years of work.
topics: Bill Bryson A Walk in the Woods

segments.title: Earl Schaefer's first thru-hike
segments.summary: Earl Schaefer, a World War II veteran, became the first person to thru-hike the trail in 124 days, starting in April 1948 at Mount Oglethorpe, using minimal gear. He later hiked it in both directions and again in the late 1990s.

segments.title: Trail facts, states, and speed records
segments.summary: The trail passes through fourteen states, with Virginia the longest stretch and West Virginia the shortest. The average thru-hike takes about 165 days. Joe McConaughey set a speed record of 45 days, 12 hours and 15 minutes.

segments.title: Blazes and navigation
segments.summary: The trail is marked with white rectangular paint blazes on trees and rocks about every seventy feet, making it easy to follow.

segments.title: Planning NOBO and SOBO hikes, the bubble and flip-flopping
segments.summary: The hosts describe northbound and southbound timing, the spring crowd known as the bubble, and flip-flop and leapfrog strategies to hike in better weather.

segments.title: Gear, shelters, food and resupply
segments.summary: The hosts discuss ultralight tents, the roughly 250 first-come shelters spaced about eight miles apart, food needs of about two pounds a day, mail drops, zero days, and gorp. They estimate total costs at about a thousand dollars a month.

segments.title: Weather, hypothermia, water and hiker hunger
segments.summary: The hosts cover cold rain and wind causing hypothermia, heat and dehydration in summer, water purification, and the weight loss and hiker hunger after a thru-hike.

segments.title: Ticks, bears, crime statistics and trail culture
segments.summary: The hosts discuss ticks and Lyme disease, bear hangs, and injury and death statistics. They say murders on the trail are rare and sexual assault is low. They describe trail magic, the trail community, and town events like Trail Days and the half-gallon ice cream challenge.
topics: pine grove furnace ice cream challenge

segments.title: Emma Gatewood and other record holders
segments.summary: Emma Gatewood, at age 67, became the first woman to hike the trail alone and later became the first person to hike it twice. The hosts also discuss Sunny Everhart, Harvey Sutton, Juniper Netteberg and Bill Irwin.

segments.title: Listener mail: kidney donation
segments.summary: Kirby writes about donating a kidney to a family friend, describing the surgery, the three-inch incision and the recovery, and encourages listeners to join the registry.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and invite listener email.
